newsitem.title: USA: Florida officials to meet with Miami city manager.
newsitem.headline: Florida officials to meet with Miami city manager.

text.p: Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles sent representatives to meet with Miami's city manager Tuesday amid reports a state takeover of the financially strapped city was imminent.
The meeting with City Manager Ed Marquez was set for 1400 EDT, Marquez's secretary said.
While state and city officials wrangled with Miami's $68 million deficit, city inspectors fanned out in search of scofflaws who owe an estimated $1 million in unpaid garbage collection fees.
The Miami Herald reported Tuesday that the city was uncertain how many garbage customers it serves and how many accounts may be delinquent.
In some instances, property owners illegally built additions to homes, which were rented to people who do not pay for garbage pickup.

But Joseph Ruiz Jr., a Dade County solid waste official on temporary loan to the city, said the city's solid waste division had no method of checking the number of homes served against the number of bills paid.
"Something is wrong with this picture," Ruiz told the newspaper.
The disorganization in the solid waste department underscores the fiscal chaos uncovered after the former city manager and former finance director resigned to face federal corruption charges.

An interim city manager discovered the city has a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for the year that began Oct 1. Miami Mayor Joe Carollo officially notified the governor that the city had a financial crisis and said he would welcome the appointment of a state emergency board to run the city.
As of Sept 30, Miami had $170.6 million of general obligation bonds outstanding, and several series of special obligation bonds.
The city made a $10.8 million debt service payment on Tuesday and is due to make another of about $7 million next month.
After making Tuesday's debt payment, the city was left with $45 million in pooled cash. Revenue from property tax payments should enable the city to keep operating for the next couple of months.

"Looking at the cash flows, it seems like they should be able to meet most of their obligations, including debt service, into the third quarter of the fiscal year, which is the first quarter of the calendar year," said John Incorvaia, vice president for municipal finance at Moody's Investor's Service Inc.
"But unless they do something, obviously the money will run out. That doesn't preclude the state from fronting them more money like they did, but that doesn't address the structural problems."
Last month, the state advanced the city $22 million in sales tax revenues that otherwise would have been paid over six months.
Chiles has since criticized the city for failing to act quickly enough to raise garbage fees and take other steps to close the budget gap.
